answer:
The objection assumes that unless Jesus utters the exact sentence "I am God," no claim to deity has been made. But that standard would rule out most ancient claims to identity, which were made through names, actions, and categories rather than propositional slogans — and Scripture itself shows Jesus making the claim in exactly that idiom. When He says "before Abraham was, I AM" (John 8:58), He deliberately takes up the divine Name of Exodus 3:14 in a way His hearers understood immediately — they reached for stones, not clarification. That is not silence; it is the most dangerous kind of speech a first-century Jew could utter.

As for the "burden of proof" — it doesn't rest on inference from silence, but on positive testimony that Jesus received. Thomas says to the risen Christ, "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28), and Jesus does not correct him but blesses those who will believe the same. John closes his epistle calling Jesus "the true God" (1 John 5:20), the very title Jeremiah 10:10 reserves for YHWH against idols. Philippians 2:10 applies to Jesus what Isaiah 45:23 says only the LORD receives — universal worship. These are not honorific flourishes loosely draped on a man; they are Old Testament identifiers of God deliberately laid on Jesus.

Now, the texts you cite are real and must be honored, not explained away: Jesus does call the Father "my God" and say "the Father is greater than I." But this is not in tension with the above once you see the pattern the material lays out — Scripture consistently shows the Son in personal relation to the Father (praying, submitting, being sent) while also bearing the divine Name and receiving worship. The natural reading is not "mere man exalted" but "true God who has also become true man," now speaking and praying as man to His Father while never disowning the confession "my Lord and my God." The claim isn't absent from the words of Jesus; it's just spoken in the mode of divine self-disclosure — the Name, not a slogan — which is exactly the mode Israel's own Scriptures used to identify God to begin with.

transcript.content: You're right to notice that — and it's the heart of the matter, isn't it? Jesus never *once* uses the phrase "I am God" or claims to be God in so many words. Instead, he consistently directs worship and prayer *to* the Father, calls the Father "my God" (John 20:17), and says plainly "the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28). If Jesus truly were God — God the Son, equal in every way — wouldn't he have said so explicitly, especially when directly challenged about his identity? The burden seems to fall on those who claim the Trinity: you're asking us to build a complex doctrine on texts that *never actually state it*. How do you justify that leap from what Scripture says to what it doesn't?
